newsitem.title: USA: Talks between UPS, Teamsters stretch into night.
newsitem.headline: Talks between UPS, Teamsters stretch into night.

text.p: United Parcel Service and Teamster officials met late into the night on Thursday to try to settle one of the biggest U.S. strikes in 25 years as UPS signaled it might soften its previous unbending stance.

"The talks continue. They are working hard on the issues," said Susan King, a spokeswoman for Labor Secretary Alexis Herman, who played a pivotal role in reviving talks to end the costly 11-day strike.
"It does look like a long night," King added. Herman, who is not directly taking part in the talks, has canceled a Friday trip to Alabama to continue shepherding the effort.

Teamster President Ron Carey canceled a speech at a union rally by striking workers in Atlanta to remain in Washington, although his counterpart, UPS Chairman James Kelly, was not present at Thursday's talks.
King described the talks as "substantive and detailed."

Kelly had declared the dispute at an impasse on Wednesday, but earlier on Thursday, he struck a more conciliatory note on pensions and on whether UPS's "final" offer was open to change under the right conditions.

"We think the pension issue is very important for both our people and the future of our company, but as I said, there is no one or two single issues that will determine whether we're able to reach agreement," he told wire service reporters in a telephone interview from Atlanta.

The UPS chief made his comments as the cost of the strike climbed toward a half-billion dollars in lost business for the delivery service and a new public opinion poll showed a majority of the public backing the union.
Kelly said that if progress came out of Thursday's talks -- billed as informal -- it might lead UPS eventually to drop what it has called its "last, best and final" offer.
"If those informal discussions lead us to believe that the negotiations could be concluded at some point in time, then the last, best and final offer would cease to exist," he said.

Issues include the union's desire to add more full-time jobs and UPS' plan to set up a new pension fund to cover only UPS workers and replace the existing fund, covering union workers at dozens of companies, mostly trucking lines.

Richard Hurd, professor of labor studies at Cornell University, said Kelly's comments were "the first sign of any flexibility from the company since they first made their 'last, best and final' offer."
But a Teamster spokesman was cautious. "There's no real reason to jump up and down until we see what happens," Steve Trossman said.
As the informal talks continued, CNN released a poll of 819 adults showing solid support for the striking UPS drivers -- the second poll this week with that finding.
CNN found 55 percent of those surveyed supported the union, while 27 percent supported the company position.

Its survey, conducted on Aug. 12 and 13 and with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points, found that 75 percent of those questioned opposed intervention in the strike by President Bill Clinton, as does the union. Only 21 percent wanted him to intervene, as does UPS.
The strike has crippled the nation's largest package delivery company and sent thousands of businesses scrambling to find other ways to ship their goods.

The U.S. Postal Service estimated on Thursday it was receiving 15 percent to 20 percent of the 12 million-package-a-day business of UPS. It said it had hired more than 4,000 temporary workers to cope with the added volume.

Kelly's comments on Thursday seemed to improve chances for a pact to end the strike by 185,000 sorters, loaders and drivers, which UPS says is costing it $300 million a week in lost business. The company is shipping only 10 percent of its normal volume.
